title: Status Cues at the Negotiation Table
description: A dialogue simulation where the player negotiates with a counterpart whose facial structure (jaw width, brow ridge) and dynamic displays (pride posture, shame glances) broadcast dominance or submission. The player must read these status cues accurately—distinguishing honest signals from bluffing—and adjust their negotiation strategy accordingly. Each round introduces new counterparts with varying facial maturity features and status displays, testing the player's ability to navigate hierarchy without verbal concessions.

partners.name: Sandra Voss
partners.status_profile: high dominance (broad jaw, narrow eyes, erect posture)
partners.display_repertoire: direct stare, chin thrust, vocal firmness, minimal blinking

partners.name: Mark Tran
partners.status_profile: mixed signals (neotenous features but assertive gestures)
partners.display_repertoire: frequent smiles, head cants, rapid pitch shifts, gaze aversion

partners.name: Elena Rossi
partners.status_profile: high submission (large eyes, round chin, soft voice)
partners.display_repertoire: frequent blinking, downward gaze, shoulder shrugs, self-touch

choose concession, escalation, or delay based on cue reading
earn points for accurate status detection; lose leverage on misreads

title: The Signaling Arms Race: Honest vs. Bluff Displays
description: An audit file detailing the evolutionary dynamics of nonverbal signaling across species. The player reviews case files of signaling systems—cowbird threat-appeasement sequences, human flirtation blends, and primate dominance rituals—and classifies each component as honest signal, bluff, or assessment tactic. The case culminates in a human deception scenario where a job candidate's confident display must be parsed for genuine competence versus strategic over-signaling.

case_files.display_sequence: aggressive rush followed by sudden freeze with bowed head
smile + eyebrow flash + head cant + sideways glance + hair flip
case_files.function: invite qualified approach via graded status signals

case_files.display_sequence: exaggerated upright posture, prolonged stare, slowed speech
case_files.classification: bluff (costly signal but may not match actual fighting ability)

stimulus.player_task: review each case and classify each display element as honest, bluff, or assessment. Justify classification using ecological cost-benefit reasoning.

title: Display Rules Across Cultures
description: A matrix exercise comparing how five cultures encode emotional expression through display rules. The player is given a target emotion (anger, sadness, pride, embarrassment) and must predict which facial, vocal, and postural displays are amplified, suppressed, neutralized, or masked in each culture. Feedback draws on cross-cultural norms research comparing individualist vs. collectivist, high-contact vs. low-contact, and power-distance variations. Correct predictions hinge on understanding culture as an adaptational solution to ecological and social coordination problems.

stimulus.player_task: For each culture–emotion pair, select the display rule operating on each channel. Scoring is based on agreement with meta-analytic findings from Matsumoto & Hwang and Hofstede's dimension data.

title: Kangaroo Care: The First Conversation
description: A dialogue simulation set in a neonatal unit where the player, a new parent, learns to communicate with their infant through touch alone. The simulation tracks the infant's physiological state (heart rate, cortisol level, alertness) as the player chooses types of touch—affectionate, stimulating, or instrumental—and observes how each modulates the infant's gaze, crying, and rooting reflex. Research-backed feedback compares outcomes against data from Feldman et al. (2002) on kangaroo care versus traditional care, showing how early tactile bonding shapes attachment and social communication trajectories.

stimulus.setting: hospital neonatal unit, kangaroo care session

touch_options.effect_on_infant: reduced cortisol, increased alertness, more gaze at parent's face
increased heart rate, alertness peaks, may trigger rooting
neutral or calming, facilitates feeding, less gaze

developmental_outcomes: 3-month follow-up: parent sensitivity score, infant social engagement, breastfeeding duration

title: Gender and the Nonverbal Decoding Gap
description: A cue-scrubbing exercise where the player watches muted video clips of social interactions and must identify the emotional state of each target (anger, sadness, fear, happiness, disgust, surprise). After each identification, the player learns their accuracy score alongside norms from Hall (1984, 2006) meta-analyses showing female advantage in decoding (r = 0.20–0.25). The player then scrubs each clip to manipulate key cues—gender of target, gender composition of dyad (same vs. mixed-sex), and context (competitive vs. caregiving vs. flirtatious)—and observes how these moderators shift the gender gap in decoding accuracy.

stimulus.baseline_task: identify emotion from muted 5-second video clips of naturalistic social interactions

scrubbable_moderators.effect: female faces decoded more accurately by both genders (Hall, 1984)
largest gender gap in mixed-sex dyads; smallest in alone condition (LaFrance, Hecht & Paluck, 2003)
gender gap minimized in caregiving contexts; maximized in competitive contexts
gender gap largest for ambiguous cues (Farris et al., 2008)

title: FACS Lab: Facial Action Units and Physiology
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player isolates individual facial action units (AUs) from Ekman and Friesen's Facial Action Coding System—AU4 (brow lowerer), AU6 (cheek raiser), AU12 (lip corner puller), AU20 (lip stretcher), AU25 (lips part)—and observes how each combination maps to discrete emotions (anger, fear, disgust, surprise, happiness, sadness). The player then scrubs across physiological channels (heart rate, skin conductance, finger temperature, cortisol) to see how each emotional expression pattern correlates with autonomic nervous system activity, using data from Levenson (2003) and Ekman et al. (1983).

stimulus.player_task: Build facial expressions by combining AUs, then see the predicted physiological signature. Compare with canonical tables from Levenson (2003) showing anger increases heart rate and finger temperature, fear increases heart rate and cortisol, disgust decreases heart rate with increased salivation.

title: Beyond Words: Reading the Voice
description: A dialogue simulation where the player hears only audio recordings (no visual) of speakers in various social contexts—a job interview, a first date, a workplace confrontation—and must infer emotional state, truthfulness, and social identity from vocal parameters alone. Parameters available for inspection: fundamental pitch (F0), pitch variability, speech rate, amplitude, voice quality (breathy, tense, creaky), and pausing patterns. The player learns how the voice encodes identity markers (age, gender, regional accent), transient emotional states, and deception cues, drawing on research by Scott & McGettigan and Scherer's vocal affect models.

vocal_parameters.voice_quality: tense (some vocal fry on final syllables)

audio_samples.inference_question: Is this speaker: (A) confident and composed, (B) anxious and filtering answers, (C) deceptive about qualifications?
Is this speaker: (A) nervous, (B) flirtatious and engaged, (C) masking disinterest?
Is this speaker: (A) calmly authoritative, (B) suppressing anger, (C) indifferent?

title: The Gesture-Math Connection
description: A boss battle where the player must solve math problems while their hands are physically restrained, then again while permitted to gesture freely. The core conflict: Goldin-Meadow's research (2009, 2013) shows that gesturing lightens cognitive load, enables new problem-solving strategies, and reveals knowledge a learner cannot yet verbalize. The player faces a series of increasingly difficult math problems (conservation, equivalence, algebraic transformation) and must choose between gesturing or not gesturing on each attempt. The 'boss' is the cognitive load itself—measured by accuracy, response time, and self-reported mental effort—and the player discovers that gesturing reduces load by 25–40% (Goldin-Meadow et al., 2001). The final phase requires interpreting a child's gestures during a math lesson to identify whether the child is ready to learn a new concept (gesture-speech mismatch signals developmental readiness).

stimulus.predicted_results: gesture condition improves accuracy by 20% and reduces response time by 30% (Goldin-Meadow et al., 2001)

boss_phase.name: Gesture-Readiness Assessment
boss_phase.scenario: watch video of a child solving math problems; child's hands gesture while speaking
boss_phase.task: detect gesture-speech mismatch—when gestures convey a strategy different from speech, the child is ready to learn that strategy (Goldin-Meadow, 2003a)
boss_phase.win_condition: correctly identify 5/5 mismatch cases and prescribe the right next lesson

title: The Gaze Dial: Eye Behavior and Social Attention
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player watches dyadic interactions and can independently manipulate gaze parameters (mutual gaze duration, gaze aversion frequency, pupil dilation, blink rate) to see how each shift changes perceived intimacy, dominance, deception, and emotional state. Drawing on Adams & Nelson's review of eye behavior research, the player learns that mutual gaze above 60% of interaction time signals romantic interest (or threat, depending on context), gaze aversion exceeding 3 seconds signals cognitive load or deception, and pupil dilation correlates with arousal and positive evaluation (Hess, 1975). The player must calibrate each parameter to match a target social scenario (e.g., 'first date showing mutual interest' vs. 'police interrogation of a suspect hiding information').

interaction_scenarios.label: police interrogation (suspect hiding information)
interaction_scenarios.blink_rate: reduced (< 10 bpm) or increased (> 40 bpm, stress)

interaction_scenarios.label: job interview (confident candidate)
interaction_scenarios.gaze_aversion_target: patterned (look away while thinking, return while speaking)

stimulus.player_task: Adjust the gaze dial for each parameter until the displayed interaction matches the target scenario. Score based on deviation from published norms.

title: Space Invaders: Proxemics and Touch in Interaction
description: An interactive simulation where the player navigates a series of social encounters (elevator, crowded party, cross-cultural business meeting, intimate conversation) and must choose appropriate interpersonal distance and touch behavior for each. The simulation uses Hall's (1966) proxemic zones (intimate 0-18'', personal 18''-4', social 4'-12', public 12'+), combined with touch categories (affectionate, stimulating, instrumental) from Ferber et al. (2008). The player's choices affect the interaction partner's comfort, cooperation, and perception of the player. The cross-cultural module adds complexity: Latin American and Middle Eastern interactions expect closer proximity than Nordic or East Asian, and violations trigger withdrawal or negative evaluation (Matsumoto et al., 2015). Touch between same-sex dyads varies dramatically by culture and context.

environments.culture_specific: handshake is universal; bow is expected in East Asia; cheek kiss in Latin America (with known contacts)

environments.appropriate_touch: none (bow preferred over handshake if lower status)
affectionate (hand on shoulder, hug if greeting/leaving)
environments.culture_specific: male-male touch varies: accepted in Middle Eastern and Latin American; restricted in East Asian and Nordic cultures

stimulus.feedback: each choice updates a 'rapport meter' and 'discomfort meter' based on proxemic norms and touch acceptability research.

title: Primate Signals: Shared Heritage of Nonverbal Expression
description: An audit file comparing nonverbal communication systems across primates (chimpanzees, bonobos, rhesus macaques, orangutans) and humans, drawing on Parr, Micheletta & Waller's review. The player reviews video stills and spectrograms of facial expressions, vocalizations, and gestures from each species and must identify homologous expressions (e.g., the human smile from the chimpanzee bared-teeth display, the human laugh from the primate play pant). The audit also covers experimental methods used in primate research: visual paired-comparison tasks, forced-choice matching, and eye-tracking for face-processing studies. The final case examines whether primate facial expressions are emotional readouts or social tools—with findings favoring the behavioral ecology view (signals serve social motives, not emotional states).

case_file_1.title: Facial Expression Homologies
case_file_1.player_task: Match each primate display to its human homologue and proposed function.

case_file_2.title: Emotion vs. Social Motive in Primates
case_file_2.question: When a chimpanzee bares its teeth at a dominant individual, is it (A) expressing fear, (B) signaling appeasement to reduce attack probability, or (C) both?
case_file_2.evidence: Parr & Waller (2011) found that chimpanzees spontaneously produce bared-teeth displays most often when in proximity to higher-ranking individuals, not necessarily when fearful stimuli are present. Supports (B): social motive, not emotional readout.
case_file_2.verdict: Consistent with behavioral ecology view (Fridlund, 1994): displays signal projected plans of action, not internal states.

title: Measuring Nonverbal Sensitivity: The PONS and Beyond
description: A matrix exercise where the player is assessed on their ability to decode nonverbal cues across multiple channels (face, body, voice, combinations) using items modeled on the Profile of Nonverbal Sensitivity (PONS; Rosenthal et al., 1979) and the Diagnostic Analysis of Nonverbal Accuracy (DANVA; Nowicki & Duke, 1994). The player rates their confidence after each item, and the matrix compares their performance to normative data across gender (female advantage of r = .22), age (peaking in middle adulthood), and professional training (therapists, actors, and law enforcement score above population mean). The player then identifies which channel they relied on most—and the matrix reveals if they over-weighed a single channel at the expense of multisensory integration, a common error in real-world nonverbal judgment (Riggio & Darioly, 2014).

title: Room for Negotiation: Physical Environment and Nonverbal Communication
description: A simulation where the player must redesign a physical space to facilitate a desired social outcome (persuasion, collaboration, or dominance). Patterson & Quadflieg's review shows that environmental features—lighting, seating arrangement, color, temperature, spatial density—systematically influence interaction patterns. The player is given a room (conference room, interrogation cell, therapist's office, date night restaurant) and must arrange furniture, adjust lighting, set temperature, and control spatial density to optimize rapport or compliance. Each decision updates a nonverbal behavior forecast predicting how interaction partners will position themselves, how much they will gaze and touch, and whether they will feel dominant or submissive. Cross-cultural variations apply: high-contact cultures prefer closer seating and warmer environments; individualist cultures need more personal space buffers.

settings.goal: maximize persuasive outcome for negotiator seating at head of table
settings.nonverbal_forecast: rectangular table + head seat + warm lighting increases perceived dominance of seated negotiator by 20% (Mehrabian, 1976)

adjustable_elements: presence of barrier (table vs. no table)
settings.nonverbal_forecast: close distance + no barrier + rigid chair increases stress behaviors (self-touch, gaze aversion) by 35% (Inbau et al., 2013)
close seating (proxemic zone: personal/18''-4') + direct orientation increases trust ratings; Western-style distance signals coldness (Hall, 1966)

title: Reading Faces: Physiognomy, Personality, and the Kernel of Truth
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player views facial photographs and must judge personality traits (extraversion, agreeableness, dominance, trustworthiness) from appearance alone. After each judgment, the player compares their rating against the target's actual self-reported Big Five scores and learns about the 'kernel of truth'—small but significant correlations between facial structure and personality (Penton-Voak et al., 2006; r = .18–.25). The player then scrubs individual facial features (jaw width, brow prominence, eye size, lip fullness, face width-to-height ratio) to see how each alters perceived dominance and trustworthiness. The final module reveals that facial width-to-height ratio predicts CEO leadership ratings and corporate profits (Wong, Ormiston & Haselhuhn, 2011), raising ethical questions about physiognomic bias in hiring.

stimulus.known_effects: wider jaw → +1.5 dominance rating (Sell et al., 2009); larger eyes → +0.8 trustworthiness (Zebrowitz, 1997); higher fWHR → +1.2 leadership perception (Rule & Ambady, 2010)
stimulus.prompt: Facial appearance predicts some real personality traits and social outcomes. Should hiring panels use this knowledge to counteract facial bias—or does measurement itself entrench physiognomic prejudice?

title: Motion Capture: Automated Body Movement Analysis
description: A boss battle where the player takes on the role of a computer vision researcher building an automated body movement analysis system. The player must select the right feature extraction and classification approaches—spatial vs. temporal representation, silhouette-based vs. joint-tracking, hidden Markov models vs. bag-of-features—for each of four emotional expression detection tasks (anger gait, sadness posture, joy gestures, fear freezing). Each wrong choice reduces classification accuracy (measured as F1 score), and the player must achieve >80% F1 on all four tasks to 'publish' the system. The final boss is a real-world noisy environment (crowded train station) where partial occlusions, variable lighting, and multiple moving bodies require hybrid approaches combining optical flow with shape-context models (Dael et al., Camera-ready 2015; Jhuang et al., 2007).

tasks.typical_body_movement: explosive forward motion, raised shoulders, clenched fists
slow gait, dropped head, reduced arm swing, slumped posture
bouncy gait, arm raising, expansive gestures, frequent direction changes
tasks.best_classifier: Gaussian mixture model with temporal smoothing

tasks.typical_body_movement: freeze response followed by rapid retreat, hunched posture, self-protective arm positions

stimulus.final_challenge: combine optical flow + Gabor filters + shape-context model to handle occlusion and variable lighting. Achieve F1 > 0.75 on all four emotions in noisy conditions.

title: Six Heritages: Tracing the Roots of Nonverbal Science
description: A dialogue simulation where the player encounters six scholars, each representing a research heritage in nonverbal communication: rhetorical, linguistic, sociological, cultural, ethological, and psychological (Manusov). Each scholar presents a research question (e.g., 'How do politicians use gestures to persuade?' 'What are the universal facial expressions of emotion?') and the player must identify which heritage frames the question and what methodological tradition it draws from. The simulation shows how these heritages sometimes converge and sometimes compete—for example, the ethological view of expressions as evolved signals vs. the cultural view of expressions as socially constructed display rules. The player learns that reading broadly across heritages yields better research than staying within one silo.

scholars.name: Prof. Rhetorica
scholars.sample_question: How do public speakers use hand gestures to emphasize arguments?

scholars.name: Dr. Linguista
scholars.sample_question: How do paralinguistic cues like intonation and pausing structure conversation?

scholars.name: Dr. Ethologa

scholars.name: Prof. Culturalis
scholars.sample_question: How do display rules for emotion differ between individualist and collectivist cultures?

scholars.name: Dr. Psychologica
scholars.sample_question: What is the relationship between nonverbal behavior and personality traits?

scholars.name: Prof. Sociologica
scholars.sample_question: How does social status shape nonverbal dominance displays in group interactions?

title: Personality Leaks: Big Five and Nonverbal Expression
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player watches muted video clips of strangers at zero-acquaintance and must rate their personality on the Big Five (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness). The player then scrubs the clip to isolate specific nonverbal channels—facial expressions, vocal tone, posture, gesture rate, gaze—and sees how each channel individually predicts the target's self-reported personality scores. Drawing on Todd & Funder's review and Borkenau & Liebler's (1992) findings, the player learns that extraversion is the most accurately judged trait from nonverbal cues (r ~ 0.40), neuroticism the least, and that segments as short as 5 seconds yield accuracy above chance. The final module tests whether the player can outperform a simple linear model that uses only smile frequency, arm position symmetry, and speech rate to predict extraversion.

known_validities.extraversion: r = 0.40 (best predicted by gesture rate + smiling + vocal energy)

title: The Olfactory Lab: Smell as Nonverbal Communication
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player explores how scents communicate emotional and social information nonverbally. Drawing on Haviland-Jones, Wilson & Freyberg, the player scrubs across odor types (mood odors from sweat, floral scents, food aromas, synthetic pheromones) and measures of social perception (trustworthiness, attractiveness, mood, approach behavior). The station reveals that olfactory cues are processed largely subconsciously, with direct cortical projections to orbitofrontal cortex bypassing thalamic relay (Stockhorst & Pietrowsky, 2004). The player learns that human olfaction can discriminate over a trillion stimuli (Bushdid et al., 2014), that fear sweat increases disgust detection and trust behavior, and that fragrances function as 'biological search engines' organizing attention and social approach without conscious awareness.

odor_types.social_effect: increases sensory vigilance, activates amygdala, enhances threat detection
odor_types.pathway: direct olfactory → orbitofrontal cortex, no thalamic relay

odor_types.social_effect: increases positive mood, social approach behavior, smile frequency
mixed: modulates attractiveness judgments, varies by sex and context
increases trust ratings of strangers, prosocial behavior in economic games

stimulus.key_finding: self-report often fails to capture olfactory effects; participants incorporate more emotion words in narratives after peri-threshold exposure even when denying mood change (Haviland-Jones et al., 2013)

title: FACS vs. EMG: Choosing a Facial Measurement System
description: A boss battle where the player must select the optimal facial measurement system—MAX, FACS, facial EMG, automated computer vision—for four research scenarios (posed expressions, spontaneous micro-expressions, infant facial displays, cultural comparisons). Each choice has trade-offs in spatial resolution, temporal resolution, intrusiveness, and coding time. The player learns: FACS is the gold standard for comprehensive description (44 AUs, 1,700+ combinations) but takes ~100 hours to train and ~2 hours to code 1 minute of video; EMG captures sub-threshold muscle activity but only on targeted muscles; automated systems (Computer Expression Recognition Toolbox, CERT) are fast but less accurate for non-prototypical expressions. The final boss requires measuring spontaneous, dynamic facial communication in naturalistic interaction (Buck & Miller's key distinction: sender display vs. receiver communication), where the player must combine FACS coding of senders with receiver accuracy judgments to separate display from communication.

boss_levels.research_scenario: detecting micro-expressions of deception during a mock crime interview
boss_levels.recommended_system: FACS (manual or automated) — AU intensity coding needed
boss_levels.why_not_alternatives: EMG can't cover 44 AUs; MAX only for basic emotions

boss_levels.research_scenario: measuring subtle emotional reactions to subliminal stimuli
boss_levels.why_not_alternatives: FACS misses sub-threshold activity; EMG captures 10-20 μV changes invisible to video

boss_levels.research_scenario: coding infant facial expressions during still-face paradigm
boss_levels.recommended_system: MAX (Izard, 1979) — designed for infant expressions, fewer categories
boss_levels.why_not_alternatives: FACS assumes adult musculature; MAX has infant-appropriate AUs

boss_levels.research_scenario: cross-cultural comparison of spontaneous emotional displays
boss_levels.why_not_alternatives: EMG inappropriate in field; MAX too limited; automated needs cross-validated FACS training sets

stimulus.final_boss: separate display from communication — code sender facial behavior (FACS) and measure receiver accuracy in judging sender's emotion. The display-communication gap reveals that some expressive senders are poorly understood, and some inexpressive senders are accurately read.

title: Vocal Forensics: Acoustic Feature Extraction
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player extracts and interprets acoustic features from audio recordings. Using Rosenberg, Enos & Hirschberg's framework, the player isolates low-level features (fundamental frequency f0, intensity/dB, duration, speaking rate, rhythm) and voice quality measures (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio, creakiness, breathiness). The player scrubs each feature to see how it correlates with speaker states: depression (monotone f0, slow rate, creaky quality), deception (raised f0, increased jitter, fewer pauses), anger (raised intensity, fast rate, hard onsets), and trust (moderate f0, low jitter, normal rate). The station also teaches about prosodic features: pitch accent, phrasing boundaries, intonational contours. Automated extraction tools (Praat, OpenSMILE, COVAREP) are simulated, showing how different algorithms produce slightly different feature values — a source of cross-study variability.

acoustic_features.state_correlation: depression: low & flat; deception: elevated & variable; anger: elevated & steady
anger: high; sadness: low; deception: slightly elevated
anger: fast; sadness: slow; deception: variable (slower during lies, faster during truth)
creaky: depression, fatigue; breathy: intimacy, sadness; tense: anger, deception

title: Coding Gesture: From Hand to Meaning
description: A dialogue simulation where the player learns to code cospeech gestures using typologies from Church, Kelly & Wakefield. The player watches video clips of natural conversation and must classify each gesture into categories: iconic (depicting shape/action), metaphoric (depicting abstract concept), deictic (pointing), beat (rhythmic, speech-accompanying), and emblem (conventionalized, culture-specific). After classifying, the player codes gesture phases (preparation, stroke, hold, retraction) and the gesture-speech relationship (redundant, additive, displaced, mismatched). The simulation draws on Goldin-Meadow's finding that gesture-speech mismatch signals developmental readiness for learning and that cospeech gestures serve a cognitive function for the speaker (reducing cognitive load, facilitating lexical retrieval), not just a communicative function for the listener.

stimulus.coding_task: classify each gesture from video, code phase, and assess speech relationship

gesture_types.example: speaker says 'the fish was THIS big' while holding hands apart
speaker says 'the idea was completely off' while sweeping hand sideways
gesture_types.function: depicts abstract concept as spatial metaphor

gesture_types.example: speaker says 'hand me that cup' while pointing
speaker says 'every time — I — tell — you' with hand pulses on each word

title: Eye Tracking Lab: Fixations, Saccades, and Pupillometry
description: A cue-scrubbing station where the player designs an eye-tracking study and interprets ocular measures. Drawing on Marchak's review, the player selects from remote vs. tower-mounted trackers, adjusts sampling rate (30-1000 Hz), and chooses which measures to analyze: fixation count/duration (attention allocation), saccade amplitude/latency (attentional shifts), pupil diameter (cognitive load/arousal), blink rate/suppression (workload, deception), and scanpath patterns (visual strategy). The player runs simulated experiments: (1) a face-processing study measuring gaze to eyes vs. mouth; (2) a deception study comparing blink suppression during true vs. false intent (Marchak, 2013); (3) an advertising study measuring first fixation location and dwell time. The station teaches key methodological issues: data loss (10-30% typical), velocity vs. dispersion-based fixation detection, calibration quality, and the challenge of analyzing pupillary data (confound by luminance).

experiments.scenario: face processing: do people with autism look less at eyes?
experiments.measures: fixation count on eyes vs. mouth, first fixation location, dwell time
experiments.expected_result: ASD: fewer and shorter eye fixations, more mouth fixations

experiments.scenario: deception detection: blink suppression during mock crime
experiments.measures: blink rate, blink duration, blink latency, pupil dilation
experiments.expected_result: false intent: blink suppression during relevant questions, lower blink count, shorter max duration (Marchak, 2013)

experiments.scenario: advertising: visual attention to product placement
experiments.measures: time to first fixation, dwell time, fixation sequence (scanpath)
experiments.expected_result: salient products attract first fixation within 0.3s; congruent placement increases dwell by 40%

hardware_options.pros: no head restraint, easy setup, good for children

title: The Smell Lab: Methods in Odor Collection and Delivery
description: An audit file covering the rigorous methodology of human olfactory research. The player reviews case files of odor collection protocols: mood-induction via video (Chen et al., 2006) vs. naturalistic stress (sky-diving; Mujica-Parodi et al., 2009), axillary gauze pad collection with dietary and hygiene controls, frozen storage and temperature re-equilibration, and stimulus delivery via olfactometer vs. sniff jars (Freyberg, Wilson & Haviland-Jones). The player must identify threats to validity: contamination from diet/medications, menstrual cycle phase effects in female donors, bacterial growth in unfrozen samples, dose-response confounds (peri-threshold vs. supra-threshold effects). The final case compares self-report vs. narrative coding vs. behavioral observation as outcome measures, showing that olfactory effects are often invisible to self-report but appear in narrative emotion word frequency and social approach behavior.

case_files.donor_protocol: male donors, age-matched, no fragranced products for 48h, no spicy food for 24h, sterile gauze in armpit during mood induction
case_files.mood_induction: video clips (Gross & Levenson, 1995) vs. sky-diving (naturalistic; Mujica-Parodi et al., 2009)
case_files.storage: gauze pads frozen at -20°C immediately, thawed to room temperature before delivery
threats: residual deodorant/antiperspirant (antiperspirant builds up over days)
bacterial growth (odor profile changes with > 2h at room temp)

case_files.study_design: measuring odor effects on social behavior
outcome_measures: behavior: approach distance, smile frequency, conversation initiation
case_files.typical_result: self-report: no difference; narrative: +30% emotion words in fear-odor condition; behavior: +25% approach in positive-odor condition (Haviland-Jones et al., 2005)
case_files.interpretation: olfactory effects operate below conscious awareness; self-report is insensitive; behavioral and narrative measures capture effects that participants deny
